name: The Bill Doesn't Lie: Building a Live Azure Cost Dashboard
body_html:
The Bill Doesn't Lie: Building a Live Azure Cost Dashboard

If you scroll up to the nav bar, you'll notice something new, an Infrastructure page. Click it. The numbers you see are real. That's my actual Azure spend, pulled live from the Cost Management API every time the page loads.

This post is about how I built it, what broke, and why I think every cloud engineer should understand their bill.

The Problem Nobody Talks About

Most cloud tutorials teach you how to deploy things. Almost none of them teach you how to understand what those things cost. I wanted to fix that, starting with my own environment.

What I Built

Two things working together.

Part 1: Azure Cost Visibility Dashboard

A Terraform-deployed system that watches my subscription spend and fires email alerts at $50, $100, and $200 thresholds. Logic Apps handles the notification pipeline. Azure Workbooks gives me a portal-side view.

Part 2: Live Infrastructure Page

A new page on this site that calls the Azure Cost Management REST API through an Azure Function and renders real-time spend data. The dashboard has two views. The first breaks down spend by service with filter pills that let you isolate costs by resource group. The second view shows total spend per resource group with a color-coded bar chart and a breakdown table showing each group's cost and percentage of the total bill.

What Actually Broke

Nothing goes smoothly. Here's what I ran into.

The subscription ID format bug. Terraform's budget resource needs /subscriptions/<id> not just the raw UUID. One line fix, thirty minutes of confusion.

PowerShell eating my URLs. The ampersand characters in the Logic App callback URL made PowerShell think it was running multiple commands. Solved by storing the URL in a variable first.

The Azure Functions runtime ignoring my venv. Core Tools kept reaching for the global Python 3.13 install instead of my virtual environment. Fixed by explicitly pointing the runtime at the venv Python executable.

Missing dependencies in requirements.txt. I installed azure-identity and requests manually into my local venv but never added them to requirements.txt. The deployment succeeded but both functions returned 404 in production until I caught it. Always update the file, not just the environment.

Cost Management API lag. The API does not always return data immediately. Locally it showed $0.00 until the billing pipeline caught up. Knowing the difference between broken and waiting matters.

What It Looks Like Now

$48.85 spent this month. Virtual Machines are the biggest line item at around $33, which makes sense. That is the lab work. Storage and networking fill out the rest.

Switch to the resource group view and you can see exactly which project is driving spend. Every resource group I have deployed shows up with its own bar and a percentage of the total. That is the kind of visibility a business owner actually needs, not a wall of line items nobody can read.

The dashboard updates on every page load. No caching, no manual updates. Just a service principal with Cost Management Reader permissions doing its job quietly in the background.

Why This Matters Beyond My Site

In a real business environment, cloud cost visibility is a serious problem. Bills full of line items nobody can read, surprise invoices, no alerting until it is too late. The same pattern I built here, budgets, alerts, action groups, a readable dashboard, scales directly to an enterprise environment.

That is the point. Build it on your own infrastructure first. Understand every piece. Then you can apply it anywhere.

What's Next

The Infrastructure page is a foundation. Uptime history, backup status, deployment metrics. There is a lot more that can live there. I will be adding panels as I complete more projects from my roadmap.

The bill does not lie. Neither does the code.

name: The Launch: Daneondemand.com Is Live
body_html:
The First Handshake: Hello, World.

If you are reading this, the CI/CD pipeline worked. The Terraform code successfully provisioned the infrastructure, the Azure Functions are firing, and the frontend is pulling data from a global CDN.

This isn't just a resume; it's a living, breathing cloud environment.

Why I Built This

Coming from a blue-collar background, I was taught that if you're not willing to sign your name to your work, you're not doing it right. I wanted a challenge, I found myself having a hard time sticking to one thing. I would commplete something and find myself stuck looking for another project. This website has been live since April 1st but I have constantly been adding, breaking and fixing things on here for over a month to completely polish it.

I built daneondemand.com to bridge the gap between "knowing" and "doing." I have the certifications, but I didn't have the hands on to back it all up.

The Tech Stack (The "Guts")

  • Frontend: A modern React application styled with "Glassmorphism" to match my love for clean, transparent design.
  • Infrastructure: 100% defined in Terraform. I can destroy this entire site and have it back online in under five minutes with a single command.
  • Backend: Serverless Azure Functions written in Python, handling the visitor telemetry.
  • Database: Cosmos DB (NoSQL) for high-speed, global data storage.
  • CI/CD: GitHub Actions handles the heavy lifting—every time I push code, Azure automatically rebuilds and deploys the site.

The "Live" Proof

Scroll down to the footer. You’ll see a Service Health Dashboard. It’s pulling real-time data from the GitHub API and Azure to show you exactly when I last touched this code and the health of the East US region.

What’s Next?

This site is Phase 2. I’m currently deep-diving into more features to add to this website. I've probably told my girlfriend that the website is ready tomorrow ever since the start of May and I've kept pushing it off to add in new features. I wanted it to be something I'm proud of and have a nice base to build off of before pushing it to the rest of the world.

Things I want to add:

    1. Interactive Progress Page: It's very easy to say I'm doing x y and z but it's better to have actual proof. I'm not exactly sure what it's going to look like but I definitely want a way to document my goals for the week, month & year. Whether that is professional or personal, both will probably be included. Also any certifications I'm currently pursuing
    1. In tandem with the above, I might have a sort of Today I learned or the issues I worked through on a certain project all consolidated into a nice page. Anything I may have learned, my thought process and how I fixed it. Also how my certification progress is going.
    1. Azure FinOps dashboard: I plan on pulling data from the azure billing api to show the monthly cost of the website. I think it's a great way to showcase a cost-effective approach that I can apply to a future employer's environment with the idea of getting the job done, the most cost effective way.
    1. Media Lab: I want to use Loom to create short little walkthroughs of labs or projects that I do. It's one thing to build, it's another to be willing to record it and walk through it. Some people enjoy watching instead of reading. I may also one day decide I want to post on Youtube, whether that is giving back knowledge or something else, I'm not entirely sure yet. I'm a quiet person, and I rarely post on social media so that's a giant leap right now.
    1. Dark Mode: Obvious reasons. This will probably be the first thing I do once I make the progress page. I don't want to touch it touch cause it might mess things up and I'm not ready for that right now.

I’m settled in Florida, my dachshund is keeping morale high, and I’m ready for my next jump into a full-time Cloud Engineering role.

Let me know what you think, email me at the bottom or message me on LinkedIn.

name: The Long Game: My Azure Roadmap
body_html:
More Than Just a Cloud Resume

My journey into Azure wasn't a straight lin, it was a battle of attrition. I started studying for the AZ-104 in February 2025. By July, I was starting my degree at WGU and working at Baird, learning what it meant to operate in a massive corporate environment.

The Price of Admission

I failed the AZ-104 twice. The first time was a 659. The second was a 646. Most people would have pivoted to something easier, but I went back to the basics. I picked up the Learn to Cloud guide, dove into Python and Linux, and kept my head down.

On January 3rd, 2026, I finally saw that "PASS" on the screen. It wasn't just a certification; it was the green light to finally build what I had been imagining.

The Florida Chapter

Moving from Wisconsin to Florida while extending my contract at Baird was a whirlwind, but it solidified my focus. I’m no longer content just closing end-user tickets. I’ve built the foundation, and now I’m looking to manage the skyscraper.

Current Milestones:

  • Infrastructure as Code: Strictly using Terraform to ensure my labs are repeatable and documented. No more "Click-Ops."
  • Observability: Integrating Splunk and Nessus because a cloud environment you can't monitor is just a disaster waiting to happen.
  • Proactive Engineering: Shifting from "Fixing what broke" to "Building so it doesn't break."

The "Cloud Resume Challenge" was the catalyst, but the journey to becoming a Senior Architect is built on these small, automated steps. I’m healthy, I’m consistent, and I’m ready for the next jump.

name: Blue Collar Logic: Why I Sign My Code
body_html:
From the Pavement to the Cloud

In the trades, you learn quickly that there is no undo button. If you seal a driveway or set a pool foundation incorrectly, you’re spending the next week fixing a costly mistake. My first job was between 50-84 hours a week of manual labor. All I knew was the crew I worked on, and couldn't wait for my hot shower & cold bed only to do it all over again the next day. The biggest lesson I took away wasn't how to fill a crack in asphalt it was ownership.

The Tinkerer’s Spirit

I spent years in logistics, CNC machining, and even considered physical therapy. I loved biology and pharmacology because I’ve always been obsessed with how complex systems work. But during the 12-hour COVID shifts in the machine shop, I realized my "tinkering" belonged in the digital world.

The First Handshake

I dropped out of my first semester of college because life happened, but that single semester was enough to land me a Help Desk role. I went from 12-hour shifts on a shop floor to 8-hour shifts at a desk, and I felt like I had found a cheat code. I started exploring everything: TryHackMe, HackTheBox, and GRC.

But I found myself bored with just analyzing. I wanted to build

Why Cloud Architecture?

I can't pinpoint the exact moment I chose Cloud, but I remember the feeling of the Cloud Resume Challenge. It was the first time a technical project made me feel the same way a hard day in the trades did. It was difficult, it required a foundation, and if you messed up the networking, the whole thing collapsed.

I've trading my shovel for a mopuse & keyboard, but the mindset is the same: Do it right the first time.
